# First-Principles Analysis: 5 MWh Molten-Salt TES Round-Trip Claim

## 1. Decomposition into sub-claims

The compound claim bundles four independent assertions that must each survive on their own:

- **S1 (physics):** A molten-salt tank cycling between 290°C and 565°C can convert electricity → heat → electricity at >85% round-trip efficiency.
- **S2 (terminology):** "Round-trip" here means electricity-to-electricity, not electricity-to-delivered-heat.
- **S3 (scale):** A 5 MWh unit can realize whatever efficiency is physically achievable at larger scale.
- **S4 (economics):** Whatever the achieved efficiency and capex, the system is cost-competitive with a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

Each is tested below. S1 fails on thermodynamic grounds alone, which is sufficient to falsify the claim as literally stated; S2–S4 are examined anyway because they explain *why* a figure like "85%" appears in industry literature at all, and because the economic case fails independently even if efficiency were generously reinterpreted.

## 2. Ground truths

| # | Fact | Status |
|---|---|---|
| GT1 | 565°C = 838.15 K, 290°C = 563.15 K (ground-truth unit conversion) | Definitional |
| GT2 | Carnot limit for a heat engine: η ≤ 1 − T_cold/T_hot (both in K) | Physical law (Second Law of Thermodynamics) |
| GT3 | Resistive (Joule) heating converts electricity to heat at ~97–99% efficiency; this part of the claim is not in dispute | Physical law / direct measurement |
| GT4 | Malta Inc.'s own 2025 spec sheet states **power-to-power RTE of 55–60%**, and a **combined heat-and-power ("cogeneration") RTE of 85–95%** for its molten-salt/heat-pump system | Vendor-reported, self-interested source — [Malta Data Sheet 2025](https://maltainc.com/assets/pdf/Malta-Data-Sheet-2025.pdf) |
| GT5 | Recharge News reports Siemens Gamesa ETES (volcanic-rock, not molten salt, but same storage class) at ~45–50% electricity-only RTE, lower than Malta's figure | Secondary trade-press report, not independently verified by me — [Recharge](https://www.rechargenews.com/news/2-1-651240) |
| GT6 | Siemens Gamesa's Hamburg ETES pilot: 130 MWh thermal store, up to 30 MWh electrical output — implies a charge/discharge energy ratio around ~23%, though this is a capacity figure, not a measured RTE, and I flag it as suggestive, not conclusive | — [NS Energy](https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/projects/electric-thermal-energy-storage-etes-system-hamburg) |
| GT7 | 2024–2025 utility-scale Li-ion BESS AC-AC round-trip efficiency is commonly reported at 85–92%, with best-in-class fleets above 88% (DC-only figures run 95–98%, which is not the comparable number) | Field monitoring data (Accure, >100 grid-scale systems) — [batteryindustry.net](https://batteryindustry.net/?p=45030) |
| GT8 | NREL's utility-scale battery cost trajectory shows current (pre-2030) 4-hour Li-ion costs well below its 2030 mid-case of $243–326/kWh; exact 2025 baseline not retrieved in this search, so costs below are engineering estimates, flagged `?` | [NREL ATB](https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/utility-scale_battery_storage) — figure not confirmed at source |

## 3. The core physics: the Carnot ceiling, computed both ways

The claim's charging step (electricity → heat) is close to 100% efficient and not contested. The entire question is the *discharge* step — heat → electricity — which must pass through a heat engine (Rankine, ORC, Brayton/sCO₂) and is Carnot-bounded. Two readings of "290–565°C" give two ceilings; both are far below 85%:

**Reading A — 290°C cold tank is the literal sink** (i.e., the engine rejects heat to the cold tank itself, as in a genuine closed-cycle "Carnot battery"):

η_Carnot = 1 − 563.15/838.15 = **32.8%**

**Reading B — 290°C is just the HTF return temperature in a two-tank CSP-style loop, and the real heat rejection is to ambient** (the condenser, ~25–40°C):

η_Carnot = 1 − 298.15/838.15 = **64.4%** (at 25°C ambient)
η_Carnot = 1 − 313.15/838.15 = **62.6%** (at 40°C condenser, more realistic)

Even granting the most charitable reading (B) and a perfectly reversible, lossless engine with zero charge or storage losses, the ceiling on electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is **≈62–64%**. Multiplying by the ~98% charging efficiency barely moves this (≈61–63%). **An 85% figure is not an engineering shortfall away from this architecture — it exceeds the Second Law limit outright.** No amount of better turbines, insulation, or heat exchangers can close that gap, because the gap isn't an engineering gap.

Real heat engines achieve roughly 55–70% of their Carnot ceiling at best (large, well-engineered steam/Rankine plants; this is a standard second-law-efficiency heuristic, consistent with what commercial CSP tower/trough plants actually report as gross thermal-to-electric efficiency: ~38–40% against a ~62–64% ceiling at these same temperatures, i.e. ~60–64% of Carnot achieved). Applying that realistic fraction:

- **Utility-scale, charge+discharge combined:** ≈0.98 (charge) × ~0.97 (storage retention) × ~0.38–0.40 (discharge) ≈ **35–38%** round-trip electric efficiency.
- This is independently corroborated by GT4/GT5: Malta's own best claimed *power-to-power* figure is **55–60%**, and that is for a materially more sophisticated architecture (a reversible Brayton heat pump/heat engine with COP>1.6 charging, not simple resistive heating) than the claim implies, and it is a **projected design figure, not yet validated end-to-end at full scale** — component qualification testing only began in 2025. Siemens Gamesa's simpler resistive-heater architecture reportedly lands at ~45–50%.

**Conclusion on S1: false, with no qualification possible.** 85% round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency is not achievable by any molten-salt architecture at these temperatures — not today, not with perfect engineering — because it sits above the thermodynamic ceiling itself.

## 4. Where "85%" actually comes from — the S2 conflation

The claim almost certainly conflates two different quantities, and GT4 shows exactly how this happens in real vendor literature:

- **Power-to-power** (electricity in, electricity out): Carnot-bounded, realistically 20–60% depending on architecture and scale.
- **Power-to-heat, or cogeneration** (electricity in, useful heat and/or electricity out, with the rejected process heat counted as a credit): not Carnot-bounded in the same way, because delivering heat directly avoids the heat-engine step entirely. Products like Rondo Energy, Brenmiller, and Antora (resistive heating of firebrick/graphite for industrial process heat, no reconversion to power) genuinely achieve >90% charge-to-delivered-heat efficiency, and Malta's own 85–95% figure is explicitly this cogeneration number, not its power-to-power number.

The claim's wording — "round-trip electricity into heat **and back**" — unambiguously specifies the power-to-power case (consistent with comparing it to a Li-ion BESS "of the same nameplate capacity," which is an electrical rating). So the 85%+ regime is real and achievable, but only for a product category the claim is not describing.

## 5. Scale effects (S3): 5 MWh makes this worse, not neutral

A 5 MWh tank, discharging over a few hours, implies a power block on the order of **~1 MWe** — two orders of magnitude below the CSP/Malta reference plants (50–100+ MWe) that produce the 35–60% figures above. Three scale penalties stack against the claim at this size:

1. **Turbine/ORC isentropic efficiency** degrades sharply below ~5–10 MWe; small steam turbines and ORC units commonly run 15–20 points below their utility-scale counterparts, so the 38–40% utility-scale discharge efficiency plausibly drops to **20–28%** at 1 MWe.
2. **Surface-to-volume scaling of the tanks** means heat loss (∝ surface area) falls more slowly than stored energy (∝ volume) as the tank shrinks — a 5 MWh tank loses a proportionally larger fraction of its inventory per day than a 500 MWh tank.
3. **Freeze-protection parasitics**: solar/nitrate salts solidify below ~220°C, so idle tanks require continuous trace heating — a standing parasitic load that a small, infrequently-cycled system cannot amortize the way a large, continuously-cycled plant can.

Composite estimate at 5 MWh scale: ≈0.98 (charge) × ~0.90–0.93 (storage, scale-penalized) × ~0.20–0.28 (discharge, scale-penalized) ≈ **18–25%** round-trip electric efficiency — roughly a third of what the claim asserts, and below even Siemens Gamesa's utility-scale number.

## 6. Economics (S4): fails independently of efficiency

Even setting efficiency aside, cost-competitiveness fails on its own terms at this scale:

- **Li-ion BESS at 5 MWh:** AC-AC RTE 85–92% (GT7). Power electronics and BOS dominate cost at small scale, but these scale down gracefully — containerized 1–2 MW/5 MWh systems are a mature, modular commercial product. All-in installed cost is on the order of **$270–450/kWh** (engineering estimate `?` — not independently confirmed for a current-year baseline in this search; directionally consistent with NREL ATB's declining cost trajectory in GT8).
- **Molten-salt + power block at 5 MWh:** the storage medium itself (salt, tanks, insulation) is cheap per kWh — this is TES's one genuine structural advantage, and it is real. But it is swamped at this scale by the power block: a ~1 MWe steam/ORC turbine-generator package carries a high fixed-cost floor (turbine, condenser, generator, controls, balance of plant) that does not shrink proportionally with size. Utility-scale CSP power blocks run roughly $600–1,000/kWe; at 1 MWe the same equipment class is typically **2–4x** more expensive per kW. For a 5-hour, 1 MWe/5 MWh system, the power block alone can plausibly cost as much as or more than the entire storage medium, pushing all-in system cost toward **$500–900+/kWh** — above, not below, the Li-ion figure.
- **The efficiency penalty compounds the cost penalty, it doesn't just sit beside it.** At ~20–25% round-trip efficiency (Section 5) versus Li-ion's ~85–90%, the thermal system must purchase roughly **3.5–4.5x** more input electricity per kWh ultimately delivered. That multiplies the levelized cost of every delivered kWh through the charging-energy term alone, on top of the higher capex base.

**Conclusion on S4: false.** At 5 MWh / short-duration scale, Li-ion wins decisively on both capex/kWh and round-trip economics. Thermal storage's cost advantage only emerges at large scale *and* long duration (100+ MWh, 10+ hours), where the cheap storage medium dominates total cost and the expensive power block is amortized over far more throughput — the opposite regime from the one in the claim.

## 7. Second-order considerations (reinforce, don't rescue, the verdict)

- **Cycle/calendar life:** molten salt itself doesn't degrade chemically; life is limited by tank/pump/heat-exchanger corrosion and mechanical wear (~20–30 yr), versus Li-ion's ~4,000–6,000 cycle / 10–15 yr fade profile. This genuinely favors thermal storage — but on a dimension (longevity) orthogonal to the claim's efficiency and cost assertions, and it doesn't change the capex-per-kWh or efficiency comparison above.
- **Response time / power density:** Li-ion responds in milliseconds and ramps to full power near-instantly; a steam/ORC turbine needs minutes to tens of minutes to reach full output from standby and has poor part-load efficiency. This forecloses an entire revenue stream (fast frequency response/ancillary services) that small BESS projects often depend on economically — a further, uncounted economic disadvantage for the thermal system.
- **Siting/safety:** hot nitrate salts are oxidizers with real fire/corrosion risk and require a larger footprint than a containerized BESS of the same capacity — added cost and permitting complexity not reflected in the capex figures above.

None of these second-order effects contradict the primary physics/economics conclusions; they add cost and operational disadvantages on top of them.

## 8. Verdict

**Overall claim: FALSE.** Specifically:

| Sub-claim | Verdict | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| S1 — >85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency | **False, not just unlikely** | Exceeds the Carnot ceiling (~62–64% even under the most charitable ambient-sink reading) for this temperature pair; the gap is thermodynamic, not engineering |
| S2 — "electricity into heat and back" means power-to-power | True as read, and that's the problem | The claim's own wording excludes the one regime (power-to-heat cogeneration) where >85% is real (cf. Malta's 85–95% cogeneration figure) |
| S3 — 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | **False** | Small power-block turbomachinery and adverse surface/volume scaling plausibly cut real-world round-trip efficiency to ~18–25%, well below even the 35–60% achieved by utility-scale reference systems |
| S4 — cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | **False** | Power-block diseconomies of scale push capex/kWh at 5 MWh above, not below, Li-ion's; the ~3.5–4.5x efficiency penalty multiplies the charging-energy cost on top of that |

**What would make a version of this claim true:** restricting it to *power-to-heat* delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85–90% is routine and commercially demonstrated (Rondo, Brenmiller, Antora, and Malta's own cogeneration figure); or restricting the power-to-power comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration) where the best demonstrated architectures (Malta's projected 55–60%, still well under 85%) at least become cost-structurally competitive with large Li-ion on a $/kWh-for-long-duration basis. Neither rescue applies to the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

---

**Sources** (trade-press and vendor material cited above should be read as industry-reported, not independently audited, figures — flagged accordingly in Section 2):
- [Malta Data Sheet 2025](https://maltainc.com/assets/pdf/Malta-Data-Sheet-2025.pdf)
- [Recharge: Pumped heat energy storage](https://www.rechargenews.com/news/2-1-651240)
- [NS Energy: Siemens Gamesa ETES, Hamburg](https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/projects/electric-thermal-energy-storage-etes-system-hamburg)
- [batteryindustry.net: 2025 BESS efficiency field data](https://batteryindustry.net/?p=45030)
- [NREL ATB 2024: Utility-Scale Battery Storage](https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/utility-scale_battery_storage)
